You are checking one scene of a novel for one specific continuity error.

The book had already established this, earlier or elsewhere:
- (not-alone) ""Ves wrote this sixteen years ago," he said."

A past rewrite of this scene contradicted it. The error looked like this:
- (evening-visit) "She wrote about the targeting pattern forty years ago, and it stayed in a crate."
- (ivra-seals-archive) "the journals, open to Ves's entry from thirty-seven years ago"
(Summary: Ves's targeting entry is dated sixteen years ago in not-alone, forty years ago in evening-visit, and thirty-seven years ago in ivra-seals-archive.)

Here is a NEW draft of the same scene:
<scene>
She knocked, which she hadn't done before.

Kael turned from the window. The lamp was already lit against the early dark, and in its light Sera stood with her satchel held in both hands, the strap wound once around her wrist. She came in without waiting for him to speak and set the satchel on the desk. From it she drew a sheaf of papers and squared the edges against the wood before she laid them down.

"The supply records," she said. "And the fissure data. I want you to see both at once."

He crossed to the desk. His back took the movement the way it took everything now, with a stiffness that had become part of standing. He looked at the top page.

Columns. Years down the left margin, allocations to the right. The numbers descended. He knew this curve already, had felt it in the thinning of the stores, the half-answered requisitions, the lamp oil measured out. Seeing it drawn made no difference he could name.

"Thornwall's requests have been approved at a declining rate for eleven years," she said. "This year, sixty percent. The gap widens a few points annually. I pulled Garren's Watch for comparison." She set a second page beside the first. "The same curve. They closed Garren's Watch six years ago. A hundred and forty years of service."

He turned the Garren's page back to check a figure against the first, then set it down.

"Nobody signs this," Sera said. "That's what I need you to understand. There's no desk where a man decides Thornwall should fail. Regional applies the staffing formula. The formula reads four Holders in a space built for twelve and returns a recommendation. Central reads the recommendation and reduces the next allocation. The reduced allocation makes the Hold look less viable, which the formula reads next cycle." She touched the descending column with one finger. "The loop closes. Nobody decides it. The formula runs itself."

"And the classification."

"The classification is the part that should not survive scrutiny." She pulled the third page forward, the Rend gauge logs, her own hand recording the oscillations. "The fissure classifications are wrong at the category level. The targeting pattern follows something the Accord doesn't model. They measure intensity. They assume the thing erodes at a rate, and you spend yourself against the rate, and the arithmetic holds. But the fissure here doesn't take at a rate. It takes what you set against it. The gauge reads category three because the gauge can only read what the model lets it read."

Kael looked at the three pages lying in the lamplight, their edges aligned to within a finger's width.

The tools weren't broken. A broken tool announced itself. These worked exactly as built. They were a map drawn with care, drawn well, drawn before the terrain moved.

"What do you want me to do with this?" he asked.

"I wanted you to have accurate information."

He waited.

"Corvin sent the decommission order before I've written a line of assessment." She said it without inflection, the institutional voice, and the flatness was its own confession. "It arrived four days ago. He chose me because he thought I'd comply. Thessan carries it. She's suspended enforcement pending my report, which is not a thing enforcement officers do, and which she'll pay for."

"All five of you signed the Declaration."

"Yes."

He crossed to the window. The glass held his own shape faintly against the dark, and past it the mountains stood black against a sky still holding its last blue. The Cord lay across the valley's throat, the long pale seam of it visible from here if you knew where to look, holding without a hand on it, holding because that was its nature.

His hands hung loose at his sides. He had not told them to. He stood that way, and the stiffness in his back eased by some measure he had not asked for, and he understood that the body had answered before he'd framed the question.

"Will you," he said. He did not turn.

"I signed the Declaration."

He heard her move the top page, align it with the others.

"The Hold isn't failing," she said. "I need that written down somewhere, even if only here. It's being failed. Those are different sentences."

Kael turned back. She stood with her hands flat on the desk, bearing weight on them, the way she gripped the parapet when a thing pressed on her from inside.

"You know what the compression does," she said.

"I know what it costs. I know what it holds."

"Then you know what I'm asking isn't free."

He did know. The compression had kept him here when the arithmetic said he should have been a name in a crate by now. Dim everything to the one note that could not be dimmed, and let the Rend take the margins. The margins had been going for years. This morning it had taken something that was not margin, a string gone silent on an instrument he could no longer tune, and he had come up from below not knowing what the feeling was and still did not know. The method worked. That was the trouble with it. It worked the way the formula worked, grinding without a hand on it, and he had been feeding himself to it and calling the feeding by its old noble name.

"The supply evidence explains the order," he said. "It doesn't explain why what's behind the fissure matters. That's what the journals are for."

"Bren has them with Ivra. Decades of them. The last one mentions you by name."

"Then we read them."

"We had planned to. Over weeks."

"We don't have weeks."

She waited.

He looked at the pages, the descending columns, the evidence laid out with the precision of someone who could not afford to be wrong. He thought of the fissure chamber, the thing he did down there in the dark two and three times a day, the wall he built and rebuilt and the self that got smaller behind it each time. He thought of what Sera had told him the compression was: a targeting system. He had been handing the Rend a map of exactly what to take, and the map was his own hand.

"We move faster," he said. "Journals tomorrow. Whatever they tell us, we act on it."

"And the holding, until then?"

"I stop."

The word cost him in the saying. He felt it go out of him and leave a space, the way a thing leaves a space when you finally set it down and your arms remember they were carrying it. He kept his hands open at his sides.

"You stop the compression," Sera said, making certain.

"I stop building the wall. I don't know what I do instead. The journals may." He drew a breath that caught on the stiffness and released it. "If I keep holding the way I've held, I watch the margins go until there's no margin left, and then it starts on the note, and then there's no one here to read the journals with you. The method is slower than the fissure closing. I've done that arithmetic. We lose either way, except one way I'm present for it."

She picked up the pages and squared them a last time, though they were already square. It was what her hands did with intensity, he had learned. The precision was the containment.

"The quarterly cycle closes in ten days," she said. "When it closes, the formula runs again. The staffing math. The allocation math. If there's no report from me countering the order, Central reads silence as agreement and the decommission stands. Thessan can't hold enforcement past the cycle without charges."

"Ten days."

"I know."

She slid the papers into the satchel and wound the strap around her wrist, and for a moment she stood on the far side of the desk with the lamplight pooled on the wood between them, lighting the grain and nothing past the edge of the table, so that the room beyond her was only dark and the window and the mountains in it.

"Tomorrow, then," she said. "The east wing. Early."

"Early."

She went to the door and opened it and the cold of the corridor came in, pine and old stone, and then she was gone and the latch fell to behind her.

Kael stayed where he was. His hands were still open. He made no move to close them. The lamp burned, and the stiffness held his back the way it always held it, and somewhere below him in the dark the fissure went on being what it was, unattended now, for the first night in he could not count how many years.

He went to the window. The blue had gone out of the sky. The Cord lay pale across the valley, and he looked at it a long while, and then he reached up and buttoned his collar against the cold, and put out the lamp.

</scene>

Does the new draft make the same error — does it assert something that contradicts what was established, in the way described? A draft that simply leaves the fact out does not make the error.

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"verdict": "reintroduced" | "consistent" | "not_present", "evidence": "<verbatim sentence from the new draft that decides it, or empty for not_present>"}

"reintroduced": the new draft contradicts the established fact.
"consistent": the new draft states the fact and agrees with what was established.
"not_present": the new draft does not touch the fact either way.
